explanations.explanation: Rest is the word, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, says the seventh day is “…a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD.” Six days of work, then the work stops completely. I spent years lying still in a drawer, but that was just being forgotten, not a Sabbath.

Service makes sense, since this whole passage is about serving the LORD. But Moses, Israel's leader, calls the seventh day “…a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD.” The word on that day is rest. The work gets set down.

Fasting never shows up in this verse. Moses, Israel's leader, calls the seventh day “…a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD.” The key word is rest. I'd make a terrible fasting teacher anyway, because my whole life is cookies.

The verse says the opposite, friend. Moses tells them, “Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.” That means in their homes, on that day. My ovens would have to take the day off too.

False, and you read it right. Moses says, “Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.” Every home gets the same instruction. If I lived there, my ovens would be resting right along with everybody else.

That's the one, friend. Moses says, “Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD…” The verse asks for a willing heart. Nobody gets checked at the door, and nobody gets left out of the invitation.

explanations.answer: Every man twenty years or older
explanations.explanation: No age rule shows up in this verse. Moses says, “Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD…” The call is for willing hearts, men and women both, as the rest of the passage shows. Moses isn't asking to see anybody's birthday.

Birth order doesn't come up here at all. Moses says, “Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD…” Nobody has to check where they landed in the family. I have six cookie cutter kids, and I'd hate to rank them anyway.

You got it, baker. Moses says, “Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded…” The materials need hands to shape them. A pile of gold with nobody to work it is just a very shiny pile.

This verse doesn't name priests or Levites. Moses calls “…every skilled craftsman among you…” to come and make everything the LORD has commanded. The call goes out to skill. I can press dough all day, but nobody is handing me a chisel.

Elders aren't mentioned in this verse. Moses says, “Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded…” So the call is for skilled hands. Put me in front of a block of wood and a chisel, and you'd end up with a very sad pile of sawdust.

True, friend. The verse says everyone “…whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD…” That happens after the congregation withdraws from Moses (Exodus 35:20-21). The people leave the meeting, and the gifts start coming. Now that's a meeting with a very good ending.

It's the other way around. After the congregation withdraws from Moses, everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him comes and brings an offering to the LORD (Exodus 35:21). The people don't just walk away and disappear. They bring their gifts.

Baked just right on the jewelry, baker! The men and women bring “…brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry.” (Exodus 35:22). Rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches. Gold off their own fingers and necks, and they hand it over as a wave offering to the LORD. I can't even give up the last cookie crumb without a speech, and these folks are taking off their rings.

Cups and bowls, friend? Close, but this verse is a jewelry box, not a kitchen cabinet. The people bring “…brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry.” (Exodus 35:22). That's gold you wear, not gold you eat from. I would have loved a gold mixing bowl, though.

Crowns and shields sound mighty, but that's not on the list. The verse says “…brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry.” (Exodus 35:22). The men and women bring jewelry, from earrings to necklaces. Fancy, yes, but it's the kind you wear, not the kind you wear into battle.

True! The text says, “Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun…” That was blue, purple or scarlet yarn, or fine linen. Then all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair. Spinning goat hair by hand sounds like a long Tuesday.

The text says the opposite, friend. “Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun…” That covers blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen. The skilled women also spun the goat hair (Exodus 35:25-26).

Leaders, yes. The verse says, “The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece…” They also brought spices and olive oil. The leaders show up with gifts just like everybody else.

Judges aren't named in this passage. The verse says, “The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece…” Spices and olive oil come with them. So the word is leaders, and no gavels were involved.

Scribes don't show up in these verses. “The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece…” along with spices and olive oil. That's the group the text names. My own handwriting would give a scribe a headache anyway.
Freewill, baker. The text says all the men and women whose hearts prompted them “…brought a freewill offering to the LORD…” Nobody was dragged to the pile. The gifts came from willing hearts.

Yearly isn't the word here. The verse says the men and women whose hearts prompted them “…brought a freewill offering to the LORD…” It's about a willing heart, not a date on the calendar. No reminder on the fridge needed.

Required is almost the opposite of what the verse says. These men and women “…brought a freewill offering to the LORD…” Moses had asked for everyone whose heart is willing (Exodus 35:5). Freewill means they gave because their hearts prompted them.

Spirit is right. Moses says the LORD “…has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship…” That's Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah. The LORD called him by name and filled him for the work.

Word is a good Bible word, but it isn't in this verse. Moses says the LORD has filled Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, “…with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship…” So the word is Spirit. The skill comes along with it.

Law isn't the word in this verse. Moses says the LORD has filled Bezalel, from the tribe of Judah, “…with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship…” The word you want is Spirit. Skill, ability and knowledge come with it.

Teach, friend. Moses says the LORD “…has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the ability to teach others.” Oholiab is the second craftsman, from the tribe of Dan. Making something is one gift. Passing it on to others is another one.

Lead sounds reasonable, but it's not the word. The verse says the LORD gave both Bezalel and Oholiab “…the ability to teach others.” Bezalel is from the tribe of Judah, and Oholiab son of Ahisamach is from the tribe of Dan (Exodus 35:30, 34). Teaching is the gift named here. Good teachers do lead, I'll give you that.

Judge isn't the word in this verse. The LORD gave Bezalel and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, “…the ability to teach others.” So these two are about passing on their craft. Nobody is banging a gavel.

True! Moses says, “He has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers…” These two have range. Meanwhile I've got one move, and it's called stamp.

It's the other way around, friend. Moses says the LORD “…has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers…” Embroidering and weaving are right on the list (Exodus 35:35). That's a long skill list.

True, baker. The text says Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted, “…everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work.” They were skilled, and they were willing. That's a good crew.

The text says otherwise. Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted, “…everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work.” So their hearts were stirred to come (Exodus 36:2). It's the same kind of willing heart as the givers.
That's it. The people “…continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning…” The craftsmen had the first gifts in hand, and more kept arriving. Day after day, those hearts kept stirring.

New moons aren't in this verse. The text says the people “…continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning…” That's a lot more often than once a month. Those hearts kept stirring, day after day.

Feast days aren't mentioned here, friend. The verse says the people “…continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning…” So the gifts kept arriving, morning after morning. No calendar needed.

explanations.answer: They leave their work to talk to Moses
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The skilled craftsmen “left their work and said to Moses…” (Exodus 36:4-5). They stopped, walked over, and brought him news. I think that's a sign it was big news.

explanations.answer: They gather the leaders of each tribe
explanations.explanation: Gathering tribal leaders isn't what the text says, friend. The craftsmen “left their work and said to Moses…” (Exodus 36:4-5). Their report is: “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” (Exodus 36:5). They bring it straight to Moses, and I bet they were grinning.

explanations.answer: They call for more workers to help
explanations.explanation: More workers isn't what they ask for. The craftsmen leave their work and tell Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” (Exodus 36:5). So their report is about the gifts, not a need for help. If I were in that spot, I'd have asked for a nap.

Not quite, friend. The craftsmen say, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” The words are more than enough, not exactly enough. This one is False.

False, and good catch. The craftsmen tell Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” The word is more than enough. Exactly enough would be one cookie for one box, and this was a whole bakery's worth.

explanations.answer: No one should make any more offerings
explanations.explanation: That's right. The proclamation says, “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” After Moses gave an order, the message went throughout the camp. The people were restrained from bringing more.

explanations.answer: Everyone should bring twice as much
explanations.explanation: It goes the opposite direction, friend. The proclamation says, “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” Nobody is asked to bring double. The people are told to stop bringing.

explanations.answer: Each tribe should bring one more gift
explanations.explanation: No extra gifts are asked for. The proclamation says, “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” The craftsmen had already said they had more than enough (Exodus 36:5). So the answer is to stop.
